segments.text: Listening Part A. In this part of the test, you'll hear a health professional talking to a patient.
For questions 1 to 12, complete the notes with information you hear.
Now, look at the notes for Extract 1.
Extract 1. Questions 1 to 12.
You hear an orthopaedic surgeon talking to a patient named Gavin Massey.
For questions 1 to 12, complete the notes with a word or short phrase.
You now have 30 seconds to look at your notes.
Gavin, please come in.
Hi, Doctor. Thank you.
Can I start by just asking you your age, please?
And what's brought you in to see me today?
Well, when it all started, I thought it was just bad back pain.
This was around 14 months ago.
My GP thought it might be sciatica, so he referred me to a back surgeon, but after the
x-rays and an MRI, etc., they ruled that out and now they think it's coming from my right
hip.
I actually had the replacement surgery done about 16 years ago.
I was planning to see the same surgeon, but he retired a few years back.
Okay.
And can you tell me how it's been affecting you day to day?
Oh, well, it's definitely causing a lot of issues for me.
I'm an accountant and it means I can't sit for any period of time.
I'm up every 10 minutes or so and I need to stand very erect for a few minutes just to relieve the feeling of pressure I have from sitting.
I guess the greatest cause of frustration is not being able to pick up my granddaughter.
She's only two and a half and constantly asks me to and it breaks my heart to have to say no.
Then there's the sleep deprivation because I can only sleep short periods without waking up and having to change position.
And I really begrudge taking so much medication.
It just doesn't agree with my personality at all.
I know I must sound like I'm whinging, but it all accumulates.
No, not at all. I completely understand.
And so apart from that one previous operation, have you had any other major surgery?
Not really, no.
What about your general health? Any illnesses? Conditions?
Well, I mean, where do I begin? I've had high blood pressure for about 10 years now.
Of course it fluctuates, but my GP never seems quite satisfied. About five years ago I was
diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome, which obviously isn't very pleasant. Then there's
what they call adult onset asthma. That came on exactly two days after my 55th birthday,
So six years ago.
They misdiagnosed it at first because of my age, but yeah, that's another one.
And then recently, just a month ago actually, my doctor told me I have pre-diabetes.
So for that he's made me completely change my diet to try to lose a bit of weight, especially
around the belly.
I've cut out carbs completely, reduced my salt etc.
So I'm on a bit of a caveman diet now.
It's not too bad, but I do miss my bread.
Oh, sorry, there's also my eczema. I can never remember the technical term for it. It starts with a D, I think.
But basically, that mainly affects my hands, especially during the winter and drier weather.
Okay. I'll use your scans here to explain a bit about the procedure.
Firstly, I should tell you that the revision surgery typically takes at least double the time of the original operation.
Did you have any issues with the original procedure?
Look, I'm not going to lie to you.
I did have a bit of an issue the last time.
Well, it was a number of things.
Firstly, to do with the anaesthetic, the spinal block particularly.
I didn't feel comfortable with it at all.
And to be honest, the thought of having another scares the life out of me.
The recovery time also took far longer than the surgeon had anticipated.
This was a stressful process because at work I couldn't meet any deadlines
and that snowballed so much that it affected the whole company.
On top of that, it really limited my hobbies.
Even the most basic thing that only required sitting was painful at the best of times,
so I spent most days lying down.
I know that went against all the advice and I really wish I'd spent more time in physiotherapy,
but I was in agony.
Look, they are all reasonable concerns.
I'll start by answering your first.
